sections.title: Derivative as a rate of change

board_events.text: Derivative = rate of change
If $y=f(x)$, then $\frac{dy}{dx}$ is how fast $y$ changes per unit change in $x$.
If $\frac{dy}{dx}=4$, then near that instant $y$ rises 4 units for every 1-unit rise in $x$.
But most real quantities change with time $t$, and two things move at once.

board_events.text: Area depends on radius; radius depends on time. That linkage is the whole idea.
Read it aloud: how fast area changes $=$ area per unit radius $\times$ how fast radius changes.
Passing a rate through the geometry with the chain rule is exactly what related rates means.

segments.text: <curious> You learned the derivative as the slope of a curve, but it has a second, equally important identity: it is a rate of change.
When a quantity y depends on x, d y by d x tells you how fast y changes for every one unit of change in x.
So if d y by d x equals four, then right near that instant, y grows four units for each single unit that x rises.
Now here is the twist. Most real situations change with time. Two quantities move at the same moment and they are linked to each other.
Picture a stone dropped into a still pond. A circular ripple spreads outward, its radius grows, and the area it encloses grows along with it.
The area depends on the radius, and the radius depends on time. That chain of dependence is the heart of the subject.
The chain rule is the bridge between the two rates: d A by d t equals d A by d r times d r by d t.
Say it in words: how fast the area changes equals how much area changes per unit radius, times how fast the radius itself is changing.
Once you can write the quantity you care about as a function of another quantity whose rate you know, the chain rule does the rest.
<curious> Derivative ko aapne slope ki tarah seekha tha, lekin iski ek doosri pehchaan bhi hai — yeh ek rate of change hai.
Jab koi quantity y, x par depend karti hai, to d y by d x batata hai ki y, per unit x kitni tezi se change hota hai.
Agar d y by d x equals four hai, to us instant ke paas y, har ek unit x badhne par four units badhta hai.
Ab asli baat. Zyaadatar real situations time ke saath change hoti hain — do quantities ek saath move karti hain aur ek doosre se linked hoti hain.
Socho ek patthar shaant pond mein girta hai. Ek circular ripple bahar ki taraf failta hai, uska radius badhta hai, aur us se ghiri hui area bhi badhti hai.
Area radius par depend karti hai, aur radius time par. Yehi dependence ki chain is pure topic ka dil hai.
Chain rule dono rates ke beech ka bridge hai: d A by d t equals d A by d r times d r by d t.
Words mein bolo: area kitni tezi se change hoti hai, yeh barabar hai area per unit radius, times radius khud kitni tezi se change ho raha hai.
Jaise hi aap apni target quantity ko kisi aisi quantity ka function bana lete ho jiska rate pata hai, chain rule baaki kaam kar deta hai.

board_events.text: Average vs instantaneous rate
A phrase like 'how fast when the radius is 10 cm' asks for the instantaneous rate.
Differentiate first, substitute the given value afterwards.
Caution 1: differentiate with respect to time $t$, never with respect to a length.
Caution 2: plug numbers only after differentiating, or a variable becomes a constant and its rate dies.
Caution 3: a decreasing quantity carries a negative rate — keep the minus sign.
Caution 4: units travel \u2014 $\mathrm{cm/s}$ for length, $\mathrm{cm^2/s}$ for area, $\mathrm{cm^3/s}$ for volume.

segments.text: There are two flavours of rate, and telling them apart is exam-critical.
The average rate of change of y over an interval is delta y by delta x — a ratio of finite changes.
The instantaneous rate is the limit of that ratio as delta x goes to zero, which is exactly d y by d x.
Exam problems almost always want the instantaneous rate at one particular moment, like how fast the area grows when the radius is ten centimetres.
That little clause is your signal to differentiate first and substitute the value only afterwards.
Caution one: everything here changes with time, so you differentiate the geometric relation with respect to time t, not with respect to a length.
Caution two: if you plug the value in before differentiating, the radius becomes a constant and its rate simply vanishes.
Caution three: water draining, a shadow shortening, a ladder top falling — each carries a minus sign, and dropping it costs a mark.
Caution four: units travel with the rate. A length rate is centimetres per second, an area rate is centimetres squared per second, a volume rate is centimetres cubed per second.
Rate ke do flavours hote hain, aur inhe alag pehchaanna exam mein critical hai.
Average rate of change, ek interval par, delta y by delta x hota hai — finite changes ka ratio.
Instantaneous rate us ratio ki limit hai jab delta x zero ki taraf jaata hai, aur yehi exactly d y by d x hai.
Exam problems lagbhag hamesha ek particular moment ka instantaneous rate maangte hain, jaise radius ten centimetres hone par area kitni tezi se badh rahi hai.
Woh chhota sa clause aapka signal hai: pehle differentiate karo, value baad mein substitute karo.
Caution one: yahan sab kuch time ke saath change hota hai, to geometric relation ko time t ke respect mein differentiate karo, kisi length ke respect mein nahi.
Caution two: agar aap value pehle plug kar do, to radius ek constant ban jaata hai aur uska rate hi khatam ho jaata hai.
Caution three: paani nikalna, shadow chhota hona, ladder ka top girna — har ek minus sign leke aata hai, aur ise chhodna ek mark le doobta hai.
Caution four: units rate ke saath chalti hain. Length rate centimetres per second, area rate centimetres squared per second, aur volume rate centimetres cubed per second.

board_events.text: The five-step related-rates recipe
Step 1 \u2014 translate words into rates: 'increasing at 3 cm/s' means $\frac{dr}{dt}=3$.
Step 2 \u2014 write a relation linking the quantities, e.g. $A=\pi r^2$ or $x^2+y^2=\ell^2$.
Step 3 — eliminate extra variables using the geometric constraint.
A cone with $r=\frac{h}{2}$: rewrite volume in terms of $h$ alone.
Step 4 — differentiate the whole relation with respect to $t$, before any numbers go in.
Step 5 — substitute the instant's values, then attach the correct units and sign.
One driving variable plus the chain rule handles essentially every problem.

segments.text: There is no theorem to prove here — the skill is a disciplined five-step procedure, and it handles almost every related-rates question.
Step one: translate the words into rates. Increasing at three centimetres per second means d r by d t equals three; how fast is the area changing means find d A by d t.
Step two: write a relation that connects the quantities, using the geometry of the situation, like area equals pi r squared, or x squared plus y squared equals l squared.
Step three: eliminate any extra variables using a given constraint, so the quantity depends on a single driving variable.
For example, if a cone always keeps its radius equal to half its height, substitute so the volume depends on the height alone.
Step four: differentiate the entire relation with respect to time, treating every varying length as a function of time. Do this before putting in any numbers.
Step five: now substitute the instant's data, isolate the wanted rate, and attach the correct units and sign.
The general bridge you keep using is d Q by d t equals d Q by d x times d x by d t — the chain rule in time.
Reduce to one driving variable, apply the chain rule, and essentially every problem in this subtopic falls open.
Yahan koi theorem prove nahi karna — skill ek disciplined five-step procedure hai, aur yeh lagbhag har related-rates question sambhaal leti hai.
Step one: words ko rates mein translate karo. Increasing at three centimetres per second ka matlab d r by d t equals three; how fast is the area changing ka matlab d A by d t nikaalo.
Step two: ek relation likho jo quantities ko jodta ho, situation ki geometry use karke, jaise area equals pi r squared, ya x squared plus y squared equals l squared.
Step three: kisi given constraint se extra variables hatao, taaki quantity ek single driving variable par depend kare.
Jaise, agar ek cone hamesha apna radius apni height ka aadha rakhta hai, to substitute karo taaki volume sirf height par depend kare.
Step four: poori relation ko time ke respect mein differentiate karo, har varying length ko time ka function maankar. Yeh numbers daalne se pehle karo.
Step five: ab us instant ka data substitute karo, wanted rate ko isolate karo, aur sahi units aur sign lagao.
General bridge jo baar baar use hota hai: d Q by d t equals d Q by d x times d x by d t — time mein chain rule.
Ek driving variable tak reduce karo, chain rule lagao, aur is subtopic ka har problem khul jaata hai.

board_events.text: Standard rate relations

board_events.latex: V=\tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h\quad(\text{cone: reduce using the }r\text{–}h\text{ constraint})

board_events.text: Sphere sanity check: $\frac{dV}{dt}=S\cdot\frac{dr}{dt}$, since $\frac{dV}{dr}=4\pi r^2=S$.

segments.text: Here is your complete toolkit of standard rate relations, each already differentiated with respect to time.
First, the plain instantaneous rate: d y by d x evaluated at x equals a is just f dashed at a — the rate at that one point.
For a circle's area, A equals pi r squared, so d A by d t equals two pi r times d r by d t.
For a circle's circumference, C equals two pi r, so d C by d t equals two pi times d r by d t — notice the r has gone.
For a sphere's volume, V equals four-thirds pi r cubed, so d V by d t equals four pi r squared times d r by d t.
For a sphere's surface area, S equals four pi r squared, so d S by d t equals eight pi r times d r by d t.
For a cube of edge x, volume is x cubed, so d V by d t equals three x squared times d x by d t.
For a cone, volume is one-third pi r squared h; here you first reduce using the radius-height constraint, then differentiate.
A neat sphere check: d V by d t equals the surface area times d r by d t, because d V by d r is four pi r squared, which is exactly S.
Yeh raha aapka poora toolkit standard rate relations ka, har ek pehle se time ke respect mein differentiated.
Pehle, plain instantaneous rate: d y by d x jab x equals a par evaluate karo, woh bas f dashed at a hai — us ek point ka rate.
Circle ki area ke liye, A equals pi r squared, to d A by d t equals two pi r times d r by d t.
Circle ki circumference ke liye, C equals two pi r, to d C by d t equals two pi times d r by d t — dekho r gaayab ho gaya.
Sphere ke volume ke liye, V equals four-thirds pi r cubed, to d V by d t equals four pi r squared times d r by d t.
Sphere ki surface area ke liye, S equals four pi r squared, to d S by d t equals eight pi r times d r by d t.
Edge x waale cube ke liye, volume x cubed hai, to d V by d t equals three x squared times d x by d t.
Cone ke liye, volume one-third pi r squared h; yahan pehle radius-height constraint se reduce karo, phir differentiate karo.
Ek neat sphere check: d V by d t equals surface area times d r by d t, kyunki d V by d r four pi r squared hai, jo exactly S hai.

board_events.text: Expanding oil slick (CBSE level)
Radius of a circular slick grows at 3 cm/s. Find $\frac{dA}{dt}$ when $r=10$ cm.
Given $\frac{dr}{dt}=3\ \mathrm{cm/s}$; relation $A=\pi r^2$.
So $\frac{dA}{dt}=60\pi\approx 188.5\ \mathrm{cm^2/s}$.
Differentiate the relation first; substitute $r=10$ only at the end.

segments.text: Let us run the five steps on the simplest related-rates problem.
A circular oil slick on water has its radius increasing at three centimetres per second, and we want how fast the area is increasing when the radius is ten centimetres.
We are given d r by d t equals three centimetres per second, and the relation connecting area and radius is area equals pi r squared.
Differentiate with respect to time: d A by d t equals two pi r times d r by d t.
Now substitute the instant's values: two pi times ten times three, which gives sixty pi.
So the area is increasing at sixty pi centimetres squared per second, roughly one hundred eighty eight point five.
Notice the discipline: we differentiated the relation first, and only then substituted r equals ten. That order is what protects the rate.
Chalo sabse simple related-rates problem par paanch steps chalate hain.
Ek circular oil slick ka radius three centimetres per second se badh raha hai, aur humein chahiye ki radius ten centimetres hone par area kitni tezi se badh rahi hai.
Humein given hai d r by d t equals three centimetres per second, aur area aur radius ko jodne waali relation hai area equals pi r squared.
Time ke respect mein differentiate karo: d A by d t equals two pi r times d r by d t.
Ab us instant ki values substitute karo: two pi times ten times three, jo deta hai sixty pi.
To area badh rahi hai sixty pi centimetres squared per second se, lagbhag one hundred eighty eight point five.
Discipline dekho: humne pehle relation differentiate ki, aur tabhi r equals ten substitute kiya. Yehi order rate ko bachaata hai.

board_events.text: Sliding ladder (CBSE HOTS)
A 13 m ladder leans on a wall; its foot is pulled out at 2 m/s. How fast does the top slide down when the foot is 5 m out?

board_events.text: Let $x$ = foot distance, $y$ = top height. Pythagoras: $x^2+y^2=169$.
When $x=5$: $y=\sqrt{169-25}=12\ \mathrm{m}$.
Minus means falling: the top slides down at $\tfrac{5}{6}$ m/s. Dropping it loses the mark.

segments.text: Now a classic that catches students on the sign.
A thirteen metre ladder leans against a vertical wall. Its foot is pulled away at two metres per second, and we want how fast the top is sliding down when the foot is five metres from the wall.
Set it up as a right triangle: the wall is the vertical leg, the ground is the horizontal leg, and the ladder is the fixed hypotenuse.
Let x be the distance of the foot from the wall and y the height of the top. By Pythagoras, x squared plus y squared equals one hundred sixty nine.
When x is five, y equals the root of one hundred sixty nine minus twenty five, which is twelve metres.
Differentiate the relation with respect to time: two x times d x by d t plus two y times d y by d t equals zero.
Solve for the unknown rate: d y by d t equals minus x over y times d x by d t, which is minus five over twelve times two, giving minus five over six.
The minus sign means the top is falling. It slides down at five over six metres per second, about zero point eight three. Dropping that minus is the usual lost mark.
Ab ek classic jo students ko sign par pakadta hai.

Ek thirteen metre ladder ek vertical wall par leti hai. Iska foot two metres per second se bahar kheencha jaa raha hai, aur humein chahiye ki foot wall se five metres hone par top kitni tezi se neeche slide ho raha hai.
Ise ek right triangle ki tarah set karo: wall vertical leg hai, ground horizontal leg hai, aur ladder fixed hypotenuse hai.
Maano x foot ki wall se doori hai aur y top ki height. Pythagoras se, x squared plus y squared equals one hundred sixty nine.
Jab x five hai, y equals root of one hundred sixty nine minus twenty five, jo twelve metres hai.
Relation ko time ke respect mein differentiate karo: two x times d x by d t plus two y times d y by d t equals zero.
Unknown rate ke liye solve karo: d y by d t equals minus x over y times d x by d t, jo minus five over twelve times two hai, matlab minus five over six.
Minus sign ka matlab top gir raha hai. Woh five over six metres per second se neeche slide hota hai, lagbhag zero point eight three. Woh minus chhodna aam khoya hua mark hai.

board_events.text: Inflating balloon (JEE Main)
Volume grows at 100 cm$^3$/s. At $r=5$ cm find (a) $\frac{dr}{dt}$ and (b) $\frac{dS}{dt}$.
Radius grows at $\tfrac{1}{\pi}$ cm/s; surface area at 40 cm$^2$/s.
In part (b) the $\pi$ cancels \u2014 a clean whole number falls out.

segments.text: Here one known rate feeds two different unknown rates.

A spherical balloon is inflated so its volume grows at one hundred centimetres cubed per second. When the radius is five centimetres, find how fast the radius grows, and how fast the surface area grows.
Start with volume: V equals four-thirds pi r cubed, so d V by d t equals four pi r squared times d r by d t.
Solve for d r by d t: one hundred over four pi times five squared, which is one hundred over one hundred pi, giving one over pi centimetres per second.
Now the surface area: S equals four pi r squared, so d S by d t equals eight pi r times d r by d t.
Substitute: eight pi times five times one over pi. The pi cancels, leaving forty centimetres squared per second.
So the radius grows at one over pi centimetres per second, and the surface area grows at forty centimetres squared per second.
Watch how the pi cancelled in part b, leaving a clean whole number — a good sign the working is on track.
Yahan ek known rate do alag unknown rates ko feed karta hai.

Ek spherical balloon inflate hota hai taaki uska volume one hundred centimetres cubed per second se badhe. Jab radius five centimetres hai, nikaalo radius kitni tezi se badhta hai, aur surface area kitni tezi se badhti hai.
Volume se shuru karo: V equals four-thirds pi r cubed, to d V by d t equals four pi r squared times d r by d t.
d r by d t ke liye solve karo: one hundred over four pi times five squared, jo one hundred over one hundred pi hai, matlab one over pi centimetres per second.
Ab surface area: S equals four pi r squared, to d S by d t equals eight pi r times d r by d t.
Substitute karo: eight pi times five times one over pi. Pi cancel ho jaata hai, bachta hai forty centimetres squared per second.
To radius one over pi centimetres per second se badhta hai, aur surface area forty centimetres squared per second se.
Dekho kaise part b mein pi cancel hua, ek clean whole number dekar — achha signal ki working sahi chal rahi hai.

board_events.text: Filling an inverted cone (JEE Advanced)
Water is poured at 8 cm$^3$/s into a cone with $r=\frac{h}{2}$. Find $\frac{dh}{dt}$ when $h=4$ cm.

board_events.text: The constraint $r=\frac{h}{2}$ reduces the volume to a single variable.
Reduce to one variable BEFORE differentiating, or an extra unknown rate traps you.

segments.text: This is the hardest of the four, and it turns on step three of the recipe.

Water is poured into an inverted cone at eight centimetres cubed per second, and the cone always keeps its radius equal to half its water depth. Find how fast the water level rises when the depth is four centimetres.
Draw it: the cone points down, water fills the bottom, the depth is h and the surface radius is r, tied by r equals h over two.
That constraint is the key — use it to reduce the volume so it depends only on h.
Volume equals one-third pi r squared h; substitute r as h over two, and it collapses to pi h cubed over twelve.
Now differentiate with respect to time: d V by d t equals pi h squared over four times d h by d t.
Set d V by d t to eight and h to four: eight equals pi times sixteen over four times d h by d t, which is four pi times d h by d t, so d h by d t equals two over pi.
The water level rises at two over pi centimetres per second, about zero point six four. The whole trick was reducing to one variable before differentiating.
Yeh chaaron mein sabse mushkil hai, aur yeh recipe ke step three par tik-ta hai.

Ek inverted cone mein paani eight centimetres cubed per second se daala jaata hai, aur cone hamesha apna radius apni water depth ka aadha rakhta hai. Nikaalo depth four centimetres hone par water level kitni tezi se badhta hai.
Ise draw karo: cone neeche point karta hai, paani neeche bharta hai, depth h hai aur surface radius r hai, dono r equals h over two se jude hain.
Woh constraint hi chaabi hai — use karke volume ko reduce karo taaki woh sirf h par depend kare.
Volume equals one-third pi r squared h; r ko h over two substitute karo, aur yeh pi h cubed over twelve ban jaata hai.
Ab time ke respect mein differentiate karo: d V by d t equals pi h squared over four times d h by d t.
d V by d t ko eight aur h ko four set karo: eight equals pi times sixteen over four times d h by d t, jo four pi times d h by d t hai, to d h by d t equals two over pi.
Water level two over pi centimetres per second se badhta hai, lagbhag zero point six four. Poora trick tha differentiate karne se pehle ek variable tak reduce karna.

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips — rate of change

board_events.text: Pitfalls & pro-tips
Pitfall 1: substituting before differentiating turns a variable into a constant, and its rate dies.
Pitfall 2: differentiating with respect to a length instead of time $t$.
Pitfall 3: losing the sign — draining, falling, and shrinking are negative rates.
Pitfall 4: forgetting the constraint (like $r=\frac{h}{2}$) leaves an extra unknown rate.
Pro-tip: underline 'at the instant when…' — it marks exactly where the numbers go, which is last.
Mnemonic: differentiate first, plug in last.

segments.text: Let us gather the traps that cost marks, so you can dodge them by reflex.
Pitfall one, the big one: plugging the instantaneous value in first turns a variable into a constant and kills its rate. Always differentiate symbolically, then substitute.
Pitfall two: differentiating with respect to a length instead of time. The driver is t, so the chain rule must produce d r by d t terms.
Pitfall three: losing the sign. Draining tanks, falling ladder tops, and shrinking shadows all have negative rates — state and keep the minus.
Pitfall four: not reducing to one variable. Forgetting a constraint like radius equals half the height leaves an extra unknown rate and a stuck problem.
Pro-tip: underline the phrase, at the instant when, in the question. It tells you exactly where the numbers go, which is at the very end.
And keep this sphere sanity check handy: d V by d t equals the surface area times d r by d t.
<whisper> One mnemonic carries the whole subtopic: differentiate first, plug in last.
Chalo woh traps ikattha karte hain jo marks le doobte hain, taaki aap reflex se inse bach sako.
Pitfall one, sabse bada: instantaneous value pehle plug karna variable ko constant bana deta hai aur uska rate maar deta hai. Hamesha symbolically differentiate karo, phir substitute.
Pitfall two: time ke bajaye kisi length ke respect mein differentiate karna. Driver t hai, to chain rule ko d r by d t terms deni chahiye.
Pitfall three: sign khona. Nikalte tanks, girte ladder tops, aur simatti shadows sab ke negative rates hain — minus ko likho aur rakho.
Pitfall four: ek variable tak reduce na karna. Radius equals aadhi height jaisi constraint bhoolne se ek extra unknown rate aur atka hua problem reh jaata hai.
Pro-tip: question mein phrase, at the instant when, ko underline karo. Yeh batata hai numbers kahan jaate hain, jo bilkul end mein hai.
Aur yeh sphere sanity check paas rakho: d V by d t equals surface area times d r by d t.
<whisper> Ek mnemonic poora subtopic uthaata hai: differentiate first, plug in last.

sections.title: The sign of the slope decides direction

board_events.text: Monotonicity = direction of travel
Over a stretch of its domain, is the function climbing, falling, or flat?
The derivative $f'(x)$ is the slope — the direction of travel.

board_events.text: Uphill: $f'(x)>0$, function increasing. Downhill: $f'(x)<0$, function decreasing.
Momentarily flat: $f'(x)=0$.
Ghat road: the sign of the gradient, not its size, decides up or down.
Sign of $f'$ controls the direction of $f$ — that single insight is the whole subtopic.

segments.text: Picture a stock index on a trading day: from morning it climbs steadily, and after lunch it slides downhill to close.
You do not need the exact values to say that. Over a stretch of its domain, we just ask: is the function climbing, falling, or flat? That is monotonicity.
Now connect it to the derivative. f dashed of x is the slope of the curve, and slope is direction of travel.
Walk left to right along the graph and watch the tilt of the path.
Where the path tilts uphill, the slope is positive and the function is increasing; where it tilts downhill, the slope is negative and the function is decreasing.
Where the path is momentarily flat, the slope is exactly zero.
Think of driving up a ghat road: as long as the gradient stays positive you keep gaining altitude, whether the climb is steep or gentle. The sign, not the size, decides.
So the sign of f dashed controls the direction of f. That single insight is the entire subtopic.
Ek stock index ko ek trading day par socho: subah se yeh steadily chadhta hai, aur lunch ke baad close tak neeche slide karta hai.
Yeh kehne ke liye exact values ki zaroorat nahi. Domain ke ek stretch par, hum bas poochte hain: function chadh raha hai, gir raha hai, ya flat hai? Yehi monotonicity hai.
Ab ise derivative se jodo. f dashed of x curve ka slope hai, aur slope direction of travel hai.
Graph par left se right chalo aur path ka tilt dekho.
Jahan path uphill tilt karta hai, slope positive hai aur function increasing hai; jahan downhill tilt karta hai, slope negative hai aur function decreasing hai.
Jahan path momentarily flat hai, slope bilkul zero hai.
Ek ghat road par gaadi chalane ki tarah socho: jab tak gradient positive rehta hai aap altitude gain karte raho, chaahe climb steep ho ya gentle. Sign decide karta hai, size nahi.
To f dashed ka sign f ki direction control karta hai. Yeh ek insight poora subtopic hai.

sections.title: Flat spots, isolated zeros, and domain gaps

board_events.text: Subtleties that trip students
Consider $f(x)=x^3$: at $x=0$ the slope is zero, yet the curve keeps rising.
An isolated $f'=0$ does NOT break strict increase.
Caveat 1: increasing is an interval property — never say 'increasing at a point'.
Caveat 2: disconnected domains don't merge \u2014 $\tfrac{1}{x}$ falls on each side, but not across the gap.
Caveat 3: $f'(x)>0$ is sufficient, not necessary, for strict increase.
Caveat 4: the clean theorem needs $f$ continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$.

segments.text: There is an exam-critical subtlety living right at the flat spots.
<curious> Take f of x equals x cubed. At x equals zero the slope is exactly zero — so is the function stuck? Not at all; the curve keeps rising right through.
Here is why: f dashed equals three x squared, which is greater than or equal to zero everywhere, and zero only at the single point x equals zero.
So a momentary slope of zero at an isolated point does not break increasing behaviour. It is like a car cresting a tiny level patch mid-climb: instantaneously flat, still going up.
Caveat one: increasing is an interval property, not a point property. You can only call a function increasing on an interval, never at a single point.
Caveat two: disconnected domains do not merge. One over x is decreasing on the negatives and on the positives, but not across the gap at zero — the hole matters.
Caveat three: f dashed greater than zero is sufficient but not necessary for strict increase; the honest statement allows isolated zeros.
Caveat four: the clean theorem needs f continuous on the closed interval and differentiable on the open interval — do not apply it where f or its derivative fails to exist.
Ek exam-critical subtlety bilkul flat spots par baithi hai.
<curious> f of x equals x cubed lo. x equals zero par slope bilkul zero hai — to kya function ruk gaya? Bilkul nahi; curve seedha aage badhta rehta hai.
Yeh raha kyun: f dashed equals three x squared, jo har jagah zero se bada ya barabar hai, aur zero sirf ek single point x equals zero par.
To ek isolated point par zero slope increasing behaviour nahi todta. Yeh gaadi ke ek chhote level patch ko cross karne jaisa hai: instant ke liye flat, phir bhi upar chadh rahi.
Caveat one: increasing ek interval property hai, point property nahi. Aap function ko sirf ek interval par increasing keh sakte ho, kabhi ek single point par nahi.
Caveat two: disconnected domains merge nahi hote. One over x negatives par aur positives par decreasing hai, lekin zero ke gap ke aar-paar nahi — hole maayne rakhta hai.
Caveat three: f dashed zero se bada sufficient hai but necessary nahi strict increase ke liye; honest statement isolated zeros allow karta hai.
Caveat four: clean theorem ko f closed interval par continuous aur open interval par differentiable chahiye — jahan f ya uska derivative exist na kare, wahan ise mat lagao.

board_events.text: Extracting increasing/decreasing intervals
Step 1 — fix the domain; points excluded from it break the number line into separate intervals.
Step 2 \u2014 differentiate and fully factor $f'(x)$, e.g. $6(x-1)(x-2)$.
Step 3 — critical points: solve $f'(x)=0$ and note where $f'$ is undefined.
Step 4 — build a sign chart: test one convenient point in each interval.

For 'increasing on $\mathbb{R}$': skip the chart, just show $f'(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$.

segments.text: Here is the reliable five-step algorithm for extracting the intervals of monotonicity.
Step one: fix the domain. Points that are excluded, like x equals zero for one over x, break the number line into separate intervals you must never merge.
Step two: differentiate and simplify f dashed into fully factored form, for example six times x minus one times x minus two. Factored form lets you read off sign changes instantly.
Step three: find the critical points. Solve f dashed equals zero, and also note any x where f dashed does not exist — these are the only places the sign can switch.
Step four: build a sign chart. Mark the critical points on a number line and test the sign of f dashed in each interval by plugging in one convenient point.
Take the example six times x minus one times x minus two. It is positive on the far left, negative between one and two, and positive again on the far right, so f goes up, down, then up.
Step five: translate the signs. Positive f dashed means strictly increasing on that interval; negative means strictly decreasing. State the intervals cleanly.
And a shortcut: for a prove-increasing-on-the-reals question, skip the chart entirely and just show f dashed is greater than or equal to zero for every real x.
Yeh raha reliable five-step algorithm monotonicity ke intervals nikaalne ke liye.
Step one: domain fix karo. Excluded points, jaise one over x ke liye x equals zero, number line ko alag intervals mein tod dete hain jinhe kabhi merge nahi karna.
Step two: differentiate karo aur f dashed ko fully factored form mein simplify karo, jaise six times x minus one times x minus two. Factored form se sign changes turant padh sakte ho.
Step three: critical points nikaalo. f dashed equals zero solve karo, aur woh x bhi note karo jahan f dashed exist nahi karta — yehi woh jagah hain jahan sign switch ho sakta hai.
Step four: ek sign chart banao. Number line par critical points mark karo aur har interval mein ek convenient point plug karke f dashed ka sign test karo.
Example lo six times x minus one times x minus two. Yeh door left par positive hai, one aur two ke beech negative, aur phir door right par positive, to f upar, neeche, phir upar jaata hai.
Step five: signs ko translate karo. Positive f dashed ka matlab us interval par strictly increasing; negative ka matlab strictly decreasing. Intervals saaf-saaf likho.
Aur ek shortcut: prove-increasing-on-the-reals question ke liye, chart chhodo aur bas dikhao ki f dashed har real x ke liye zero se bada ya barabar hai.

board_events.text: Increasing & decreasing — definitions
On an interval $I$, take any two points $x_1<x_2$:
Strictly increasing or decreasing on $I$ means monotonic on $I$.

segments.text: Let us pin down the definitions precisely, because the difference between increasing and strictly increasing decides many marks.
Fix an interval I inside the domain, and take any two points x one less than x two.
The function is increasing on I if x one less than x two forces f of x one to be less than or equal to f of x two — note the or-equal, so flat stretches are allowed.
It is strictly increasing if that same order forces f of x one to be strictly less than f of x two, with no flat stretches.
It is decreasing if x one less than x two forces f of x one to be greater than or equal to f of x two.
And it is strictly decreasing if f of x one is strictly greater than f of x two.
A function that is strictly increasing, or strictly decreasing, on I is called monotonic on I.
Chalo definitions ko precisely pin karte hain, kyunki increasing aur strictly increasing ka farak kayi marks decide karta hai.
Domain ke andar ek interval I fix karo, aur koi bhi do points lo x one less than x two.
Function I par increasing hai agar x one less than x two f of x one ko f of x two se less than or equal to bana de — or-equal note karo, to flat stretches allowed hain.
Yeh strictly increasing hai agar wahi order f of x one ko f of x two se strictly less than bana de, bina kisi flat stretch ke.
Yeh decreasing hai agar x one less than x two f of x one ko f of x two se greater than or equal to bana de.
Aur yeh strictly decreasing hai agar f of x one, f of x two se strictly greater than ho.
Jo function I par strictly increasing, ya strictly decreasing hai, use I par monotonic kehte hain.

board_events.text: First-derivative criterion
Let $f$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. Then on $(a,b)$:

board_events.latex: f'(x)\ge 0,\ =0\ \text{at finitely many isolated points}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{still strictly increasing}

board_events.text: The sharper last version is the one that correctly handles $x^3$.

segments.text: Now the theorem that turns slopes into conclusions — the first-derivative criterion.
Require f continuous on the closed interval a to b and differentiable on the open interval. Then on that open interval the following hold.
If f dashed is positive throughout, then f is strictly increasing on the closed interval.
If f dashed is negative throughout, then f is strictly decreasing on the closed interval.
If f dashed is zero for every x, then f is constant on the interval.
And the sharper version: if f dashed is greater than or equal to zero, and equals zero only at finitely many isolated points, then f is still strictly increasing.
That last, sharper line is exactly the one that correctly handles x cubed, whose derivative touches zero at a single point yet the function keeps rising.
Ab woh theorem jo slopes ko conclusions mein badalta hai — first-derivative criterion.
f ko closed interval a se b par continuous aur open interval par differentiable rakho. Phir us open interval par yeh sab hote hain.
Agar f dashed poore mein positive hai, to f closed interval par strictly increasing hai.
Agar f dashed poore mein negative hai, to f closed interval par strictly decreasing hai.
Agar f dashed har x ke liye zero hai, to f interval par constant hai.
Aur sharper version: agar f dashed zero se bada ya barabar hai, aur zero sirf finitely many isolated points par hai, to f phir bhi strictly increasing hai.
Woh aakhri, sharper line hi exactly x cubed ko sahi handle karti hai, jiska derivative ek single point par zero chhoota hai phir bhi function chadhta rehta hai.

sections.title: Worked example — intervals for a cubic

board_events.text: Intervals of monotonicity (CBSE level)
$f(x)=2x^3-9x^2+12x+5$ on $\mathbb{R}$. Find where it is strictly increasing/decreasing.
Critical points $x=1,2$ split $\mathbb{R}$ into three intervals.
Increasing on $(-\infty,1]\cup[2,\infty)$; decreasing on $[1,2]$.
Factor $f'$ fully — the sign changes then read off instantly.

segments.text: Let us run the algorithm on the standard board question.
Take f of x equals two x cubed minus nine x squared plus twelve x plus five, defined on all real numbers, and find where it is strictly increasing and strictly decreasing.
Differentiate: f dashed equals six x squared minus eighteen x plus twelve, which factors as six times x minus one times x minus two.
Set f dashed to zero: the critical points are x equals one and x equals two, splitting the real line into three intervals.
Test one point in each: at zero f dashed is twelve, positive; at one point five it is minus one point five, negative; at three it is twelve, positive.
So f is strictly increasing on minus infinity to one and on two to infinity, and strictly decreasing on one to two.
The move that made it painless was factoring f dashed fully — the sign pattern then reads off at a glance.
Chalo standard board question par algorithm chalate hain.
f of x equals two x cubed minus nine x squared plus twelve x plus five lo, jo saare real numbers par defined hai, aur nikaalo yeh kahan strictly increasing aur strictly decreasing hai.
Differentiate karo: f dashed equals six x squared minus eighteen x plus twelve, jo six times x minus one times x minus two factor hota hai.
f dashed ko zero set karo: critical points hain x equals one aur x equals two, real line ko teen intervals mein toddte hue.
Har mein ek point test karo: zero par f dashed twelve hai, positive; one point five par minus one point five, negative; three par twelve, positive.
To f strictly increasing hai minus infinity se one par aur two se infinity par, aur strictly decreasing one se two par.
Jis move ne ise aasaan banaya woh tha f dashed ko fully factor karna — sign pattern phir ek nazar mein padh jaata hai.

sections.title: Worked example — an inequality via monotonicity

board_events.text: Proving x > log(1+x) (CBSE HOTS)
Prove $x>\log(1+x)$ for all $x>0$ using a helper function.
Define the gap $g(x)=x-\log(1+x)$ on $[0,\infty)$.
For $x>0$ both parts are positive, so $g'(x)>0$: $g$ is strictly increasing.
State 'strictly increasing' and anchor at $g(0)=0$ \u2014 the step students drop.

segments.text: Here is the favourite HOTS pattern: prove an inequality by turning it into a monotonicity statement.
We must show that x is greater than log of one plus x for every positive x.
The trick is to build a helper function whose sign we want to pin down. Let g of x equal x minus log of one plus x, on zero to infinity.
Differentiate: g dashed equals one minus one over one plus x, which simplifies to x over one plus x.
For x positive, both the numerator and the denominator are positive, so g dashed is positive, meaning g is strictly increasing on this interval.
Therefore for any positive x, g of x is greater than g of zero, and g of zero is zero minus log of one, which is zero. So x minus log of one plus x is positive, giving the inequality.
The step students drop is stating that g is strictly increasing and evaluating the anchor g of zero equals zero. The inequality is exactly the gap above that anchor.
Yeh raha favourite HOTS pattern: ek inequality ko monotonicity statement mein badalkar prove karo.
Humein dikhana hai ki x, log of one plus x se bada hai har positive x ke liye.
Trick hai ek helper function banana jiska sign hum pin karna chahte hain. Maano g of x equals x minus log of one plus x, zero se infinity par.
Differentiate karo: g dashed equals one minus one over one plus x, jo x over one plus x simplify hota hai.
x positive ke liye, numerator aur denominator dono positive hain, to g dashed positive hai, matlab g is interval par strictly increasing hai.
Isliye kisi bhi positive x ke liye, g of x, g of zero se bada hai, aur g of zero zero minus log of one hai, jo zero hai. To x minus log of one plus x positive hai, jo inequality deta hai.
Jo step students chhodte hain woh hai g ko strictly increasing kehna aur anchor g of zero equals zero evaluate karna. Inequality bilkul us anchor ke upar ka gap hai.

sections.title: Worked example — parameter for increase on the reals

board_events.text: Find k for increase on ℝ (JEE Main)
For which $k$ is $f(x)=x^3+kx^2+3x+7$ strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$?
$f'$ is an upward parabola; need $f'(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$, so its discriminant $\le 0$.
At $k=\pm3$, $\Delta=0$: $f'$ touches zero once \u2014 still strictly increasing.

segments.text: This example fuses monotonicity with the discriminant condition for a quadratic — two ideas in one.
For which real values of k is f of x equals x cubed plus k x squared plus three x plus seven strictly increasing on all of the reals?
Differentiate: f dashed equals three x squared plus two k x plus three.

For f to be strictly increasing everywhere, we need f dashed greater than or equal to zero for every x. Since f dashed is an upward parabola, it stays non-negative exactly when its discriminant is less than or equal to zero.
Compute the discriminant: two k squared minus four times three times three, which is four k squared minus thirty six, and we set it less than or equal to zero.
That gives k squared less than or equal to nine, so k lies between minus three and three inclusive.

At the endpoints k equals plus or minus three, the discriminant is zero, so f dashed touches zero at a single point and is positive elsewhere — still strictly increasing, which is why the endpoints are included.
Yeh example monotonicity ko quadratic ki discriminant condition ke saath fuse karta hai — do ideas ek mein.
Kin real values of k ke liye f of x equals x cubed plus k x squared plus three x plus seven saare reals par strictly increasing hai?
Differentiate karo: f dashed equals three x squared plus two k x plus three.

f ko har jagah strictly increasing hone ke liye, humein f dashed zero se bada ya barabar chahiye har x ke liye. Kyunki f dashed ek upward parabola hai, yeh tabhi non-negative rehta hai jab uska discriminant zero se kam ya barabar ho.
Discriminant nikaalo: two k squared minus four times three times three, jo four k squared minus thirty six hai, aur ise zero se kam ya barabar set karo.
Yeh deta hai k squared less than or equal to nine, to k minus three aur three ke beech inclusive hai.

Endpoints par k equals plus ya minus three, discriminant zero hai, to f dashed ek single point par zero chhoota hai aur baaki jagah positive — phir bhi strictly increasing, isiliye endpoints included hain.

sections.title: Worked example — a trig inequality by AM–GM

board_events.text: Show 2 sin x + tan x > 3x (JEE Advanced)
Show $2\sin x+\tan x>3x$ for all $x\in(0,\tfrac{\pi}{2})$.
Let $h(x)=2\sin x+\tan x-3x$, with $h(0)=0$.
Equality needs $\cos^3 x=1$, i.e. $x=0$ (excluded); so $h'>0$, $h$ strictly increasing, $h(x)>0$.

segments.text: The Advanced level version pairs monotonicity with a slick inequality trick.
Show that two sine x plus tan x is greater than three x for every x strictly between zero and pi over two.
Define the gap h of x as two sine x plus tan x minus three x, and note that h of zero is zero.
Differentiate: h dashed equals two cosine x plus secant squared x minus three. We claim this is positive on the open interval.

<excited> Here comes the clever move: apply the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality to the three positive numbers cosine x, cosine x, and secant squared x. Their average is at least the cube root of their product, and that product simplifies to one.
So two cosine x plus secant squared x is at least three, which means h dashed is greater than or equal to zero.

Equality in the mean inequality needs cosine cubed x equal to one, that is x equals zero, which is excluded. So h dashed is strictly positive, h is strictly increasing, and h of x exceeds h of zero, giving the inequality.
Advanced level version monotonicity ko ek slick inequality trick ke saath jodta hai.
Dikhao ki two sine x plus tan x, three x se bada hai har x ke liye jo zero aur pi over two ke beech strictly ho.
Gap h of x ko two sine x plus tan x minus three x define karo, aur note karo ki h of zero zero hai.
Differentiate karo: h dashed equals two cosine x plus secant squared x minus three. Hum claim karte hain yeh open interval par positive hai.

<excited> Ab aata hai clever move: arithmetic-geometric mean inequality lagao teen positive numbers par cosine x, cosine x, aur secant squared x. Inka average kam se kam inke product ka cube root hai, aur woh product one simplify hota hai.
To two cosine x plus secant squared x kam se kam three hai, matlab h dashed zero se bada ya barabar hai.

Mean inequality mein equality ko cosine cubed x equals one chahiye, matlab x equals zero, jo excluded hai. To h dashed strictly positive hai, h strictly increasing hai, aur h of x, h of zero se bada hai, jo inequality deta hai.

board_events.text: Pitfalls & pro-tips
Pitfall 1: merging disjoint intervals \u2014 $\tfrac{1}{x}$ falls on each side, but the union is not decreasing.
Pitfall 2: demanding $f'>0$ when $f'\ge 0$ with isolated zeros already suffices.
Pitfall 3: sign-chart slips — factor $f'$ fully and test every sub-interval.
Pitfall 4: when $f$ is continuous, closed brackets at critical points are accepted in CBSE.
Pro-tip: for 'increasing on $\mathbb{R}$', bound $f'$ \u2014 complete the square, or use $-1\le\cos x\le 1$.
Mnemonic: slope says go — positive slope, function up; negative slope, function down.

segments.text: Let us collect the traps that quietly drain marks in monotonicity questions.
Pitfall one: merging disjoint intervals. One over x is decreasing on each side of zero, but writing it as decreasing across the whole domain is false — always split at domain breaks.

Pitfall two: demanding f dashed strictly greater than zero when greater than or equal to zero, with isolated zeros, already suffices. Rejecting x cubed as not strictly increasing is the classic error.
Pitfall three: sign-chart slips — testing only one point, or losing a factor's sign. Always factor f dashed fully and test every sub-interval.
Pitfall four: endpoint paranoia. When f is continuous at a critical point, closed brackets there are accepted for strict monotonicity in the board scheme.
Pro-tip: for a prove-increasing-on-the-reals question, do not draw a chart. Bound f dashed directly — complete the square, or use that cosine lies between minus one and one.
<whisper> And the mnemonic that carries it all: slope says go. Positive slope, the function goes up; negative slope, it goes down.
Chalo woh traps ikattha karte hain jo monotonicity questions mein chupke se marks nichod lete hain.
Pitfall one: disjoint intervals merge karna. One over x zero ke dono taraf decreasing hai, lekin ise poore domain par decreasing likhna galat hai — hamesha domain breaks par split karo.
Pitfall two: f dashed strictly zero se bada maangna jab zero se bada ya barabar, isolated zeros ke saath, pehle hi kaafi hai. x cubed ko not strictly increasing bolkar reject karna classic galti hai.
Pitfall three: sign-chart slips — sirf ek point test karna, ya kisi factor ka sign khona. Hamesha f dashed fully factor karo aur har sub-interval test karo.
Pitfall four: endpoint paranoia. Jab f ek critical point par continuous hai, wahan closed brackets strict monotonicity ke liye board scheme mein accepted hain.
Pro-tip: prove-increasing-on-the-reals question ke liye, chart mat banao. f dashed ko seedha bound karo — complete the square, ya use karo ki cosine minus one aur one ke beech hai.
<whisper> Aur woh mnemonic jo sab uthaata hai: slope says go. Positive slope, function upar jaata hai; negative slope, neeche.

board_events.text: Peaks, valleys, and flat spots
A local maximum is a hilltop — higher than everything immediately around it.
A local minimum is a valley floor — lower than its immediate surroundings.

board_events.caption: A road profile: local max, local min, and the absolute max overall

board_events.text: The absolute (global) maximum/minimum is the tallest/lowest point over the whole journey.
At a smooth peak or trough the road is momentarily flat, so $f'(x)=0$.
Critical points: where $f'(c)=0$ OR $f'(c)$ does not exist (a kink).
'Tallest nearby' vs 'tallest overall' — that distinction is the heart of the subtopic.

segments.text: Think of a road trip across the Western Ghats, where your altitude rises and falls with peaks and troughs all along the way.
A local maximum is a hilltop: higher than everything immediately around it, even if a taller peak sits far down the road.
A local minimum is a valley floor: lower than its immediate surroundings.
Sketch the whole profile and you see several hilltops and valleys, plus one point that is the tallest of all.
That tallest point over the entire journey is the absolute, or global, maximum, and the lowest overall is the absolute minimum.
Now bring in the derivative. At the exact instant you crest a smooth hilltop or bottom out in a valley, the road is momentarily flat, so the slope f dashed is zero.
Those flat spots, together with any points where the road kinks and the slope is undefined, are the critical points — the only candidates for local extrema.
So hold onto the one distinction that runs through everything here: tallest nearby versus tallest overall.
Western Ghats ke ek road trip ke baare mein socho, jahan aapki altitude peaks aur troughs ke saath upar-neeche hoti rehti hai.
Ek local maximum ek hilltop hai: apne aas-paas ki har cheez se ooncha, chaahe ek taller peak door road par ho.
Ek local minimum ek valley floor hai: apne immediate surroundings se neecha.
Poora profile sketch karo to aapko kayi hilltops aur valleys dikhte hain, plus ek point jo sabse ooncha hai.
Woh sabse ooncha point poore journey par absolute, ya global, maximum hai, aur sabse neecha overall absolute minimum hai.
Ab derivative laao. Jis instant aap ek smooth hilltop par pahunchte ho ya valley mein neeche aate ho, road momentarily flat hoti hai, to slope f dashed zero hota hai.
Woh flat spots, saath mein woh points jahan road mudti hai aur slope undefined hai, critical points hain — local extrema ke lie ekmaatra candidates.
To woh ek distinction pakad ke rakho jo yahan har cheez mein chalta hai: tallest nearby versus tallest overall.

sections.title: The two tests and the inflection trap

board_events.text: First & Second Derivative Tests
Approaching a peak $f'>0$; just past it $f'<0$. The slope flips $+$ to $-$.
At a valley the slope flips $-$ to $+$. That flip certifies the extremum — the First Derivative Test.

board_events.text: Alternatively read the curvature: $f''<0$ at a peak, $f''>0$ at a valley — the Second Derivative Test.
Trap: $f(x)=x^3$ at $x=0$ has $f'=0$ but no sign flip \u2014 a point of inflection, not an extremum.
So $f'(c)=0$ is necessary but NOT sufficient for a local extremum.
And if $f''(c)=0$ the second test is silent \u2014 fall back to the first test (e.g. $x^4$ at $0$).

segments.text: There are two ways to certify a critical point, and both come straight from the derivative.
Think of the derivative as a direction sign. Approaching a hilltop you are going up, so f dashed is positive; just past it you are going down, so f dashed is negative.
At a valley it flips the other way, from negative to positive. That flip in the sign of f dashed is what actually certifies a peak or trough — this is the First Derivative Test.
You can also read the curvature instead of the slope flip.
At a hilltop the road curves downward, that is f double dashed negative; at a valley it curves upward, f double dashed positive. Reading curvature is the Second Derivative Test.

<curious> But here is the trap that catches students every exam. Take x cubed at zero: the slope is zero, the road goes flat for an instant, yet you keep climbing right through. The slope is positive before and positive after — it never flipped. That is a point of inflection, not an extremum.
So f dashed at c equal to zero is necessary but not sufficient for a local extremum — a bare flat spot proves nothing.

And when f double dashed at c is zero, the second test is silent, not negative. Fall back to the first test — for example x to the fourth at zero, whose second derivative is zero yet is clearly a minimum.
Ek critical point ko certify karne ke do tareeke hain, aur dono seedhe derivative se aate hain.
Derivative ko ek direction sign ki tarah socho. Hilltop ke paas jaate hue aap upar jaa rahe ho, to f dashed positive hai; uske thoda aage aap neeche jaa rahe ho, to f dashed negative hai.
Valley par yeh doosri taraf flip karta hai, negative se positive. f dashed ke sign ka yeh flip hi asal mein ek peak ya trough certify karta hai — yeh First Derivative Test hai.
Aap slope flip ke bajaye curvature bhi padh sakte ho.
Hilltop par road neeche curve karti hai, matlab f double dashed negative; valley par upar curve karti hai, f double dashed positive. Curvature padhna Second Derivative Test hai.

<curious> Par yeh raha woh trap jo students ko har exam pakadta hai. x cubed at zero lo: slope zero hai, road ek instant flat hoti hai, phir bhi aap seedha chadhte raho. Slope pehle positive aur baad mein positive — kabhi flip nahi hua. Yeh point of inflection hai, extremum nahi.
To f dashed at c equal to zero necessary hai but sufficient nahi ek local extremum ke liye — ek khaali flat spot kuch prove nahi karta.

Aur jab f double dashed at c zero hai, second test silent hai, negative nahi. First test par wapas jao — jaise x to the fourth at zero, jiska second derivative zero hai phir bhi clearly ek minimum hai.

sections.title: Procedures: local extrema and absolute extrema

board_events.text: Two working procedures
A) Local extrema (Second Derivative Test, fastest when $f''$ is easy):
1. Solve $f'(x)=0$ (and note where $f'$ is undefined) to get critical points.
2. Compute $f''$ at each: $f''<0$ gives a max, $f''>0$ gives a min, $f''=0$ is inconclusive.
3. Report the VALUE by substituting $c$ back into $f$, not just its location.
B) Absolute extrema on $[a,b]$ (Working Rule):
1. Find critical points inside $(a,b)$; 2. evaluate $f$ there AND at both endpoints $a,b$.
3. Compare the shortlist: largest = absolute max, smallest = absolute min. The endpoints are the step most students forget.

segments.text: Two procedures cover almost every extremum question. Start with finding local extrema, using the Second Derivative Test, which is fastest when the second derivative is easy.
Procedure A. Note it is best when f double dashed is clean to compute.
Step one: solve f dashed equal to zero, and also note any point where f dashed is undefined — those are your critical points.
Step two: compute f double dashed at each critical point. Negative gives a maximum, positive gives a minimum, and zero is inconclusive, so you switch to the first test.
Step three: report the value. Substitute the critical point back into f to state the extremum value, not just where it sits.
Procedure B handles absolute extrema on a closed interval a to b, and it runs by a simple working rule.
Step one: find all critical points inside the open interval. Step two: evaluate f at every one of them and also at both endpoints a and b.

Step three: compare the whole shortlist — the largest value is the absolute maximum, the smallest is the absolute minimum. Evaluating the endpoints is the step most students forget, because a global extreme can sit at an endpoint where the slope is not zero at all.
Do procedures lagbhag har extremum question cover karte hain. Local extrema dhoondhne se shuru karo, Second Derivative Test se, jo tab sabse fast hai jab second derivative aasaan ho.
Procedure A. Note karo yeh tab best hai jab f double dashed compute karna clean ho.
Step one: f dashed equal to zero solve karo, aur woh point bhi note karo jahan f dashed undefined hai — yehi aapke critical points hain.
Step two: har critical point par f double dashed compute karo. Negative maximum deta hai, positive minimum deta hai, aur zero inconclusive hai, to aap first test par switch karte ho.
Step three: value report karo. Critical point ko wapas f mein substitute karke extremum value batao, sirf jagah nahi.
Procedure B ek closed interval a se b par absolute extrema handle karta hai, aur yeh ek simple working rule se chalta hai.
Step one: open interval ke andar saare critical points nikaalo. Step two: f ko un har ek par evaluate karo aur dono endpoints a aur b par bhi.

Step three: poori shortlist compare karo — sabse bada value absolute maximum hai, sabse chhota absolute minimum. Endpoints evaluate karna woh step hai jo zyaadatar students bhoolte hain, kyunki global extreme ek endpoint par baith sakta hai jahan slope zero hai hi nahi.

board_events.text: Optimization: the applied form
1. Name the variables; write the quantity to optimize as a function of ONE variable.
Use any constraint to eliminate the others — calculus tools act on a single variable.
2. State the feasible domain (lengths positive, etc.) so you know which roots to keep.
3. Differentiate, solve $f'=0$, and reject roots outside the domain.
A root giving a negative length or zero volume is physically meaningless — discard it.
4. Confirm max vs min with the second or first test.
Then answer the exact question asked — often a value or a dimension, not the variable you solved for.

segments.text: Optimization word problems are just the applied form of the procedures we just built, wrapped in a story.
Step one: name your variables and write the quantity you want to optimize as a function of a single variable.
Use whatever constraint the problem gives to eliminate the other variables, because the calculus tools only act on a one-variable function.
Step two: state the feasible domain. Lengths are positive, a fraction cut cannot exceed the sheet, and so on — this tells you which critical roots to keep and whether endpoints matter.
Step three: differentiate, solve f dashed equal to zero, and reject any root that falls outside the feasible domain.
A root that gives a negative length or a zero volume is physically meaningless, so discard it without hesitation.
Step four: confirm whether you have a maximum or a minimum, using the second-derivative test or a sign test.
Finally, answer the exact question that was asked. Examiners often want the maximum value or a specific dimension, not the variable you happened to solve for.
Optimization word problems bas un procedures ka applied form hain jo humne abhi banaye, ek story mein lipte hue.
Step one: apne variables name karo aur jis quantity ko optimize karna hai use ek single variable ka function likho.
Problem jo bhi constraint deta hai use karke doosre variables hatao, kyunki calculus tools sirf ek one-variable function par act karte hain.

Step two: feasible domain batao. Lengths positive hain, kata hua tukda sheet se bada nahi ho sakta, waghairah — yeh batata hai kaunse critical roots rakhne hain aur endpoints maayne rakhte hain ya nahi.
Step three: differentiate karo, f dashed equal to zero solve karo, aur koi bhi root jo feasible domain ke bahar giré use reject karo.
Ek root jo negative length ya zero volume deta hai physically meaningless hai, to bina jhijhak use discard karo.
Step four: confirm karo ki aapke paas maximum hai ya minimum, second-derivative test ya sign test se.
Aakhir mein, jo exact question poocha gaya usका jawab do. Examiners aksar maximum value ya ek specific dimension chahte hain, na ki woh variable jo aapne solve kiya.

board_events.text: Extrema — precise definitions
Local looks at a tiny neighbourhood; absolute looks at the whole interval $[a,b]$.

segments.text: Let us state the definitions precisely, since local and absolute are genuinely different questions.
A point c is a local maximum if there is some small radius h around it on which f of c exceeds f of x for every nearby x.
A point c is a local minimum if there is some small radius h on which f of c is less than f of x for every nearby x.
For absolute extrema on a closed interval, c is an absolute maximum exactly when f of x is less than or equal to f of c for every x in the interval.
And d is an absolute minimum exactly when f of x is greater than or equal to f of d across the whole interval.
A critical point is a point in the domain where f dashed is zero, or where f dashed does not exist.
The contrast to hold: local looks only at a tiny neighbourhood, while absolute compares over the entire closed interval a to b.
Definitions ko precisely batate hain, kyunki local aur absolute sach mein alag questions hain.
Ek point c local maximum hai agar uske aas-paas koi chhota radius h ho jis par f of c har nearby x ke f of x se bada ho.
Ek point c local minimum hai agar koi chhota radius h ho jis par f of c har nearby x ke f of x se chhota ho.
Closed interval par absolute extrema ke liye, c absolute maximum tabhi hai jab interval ke har x ke liye f of x, f of c se less than or equal to ho.
Aur d absolute minimum tabhi hai jab poore interval par f of x, f of d se greater than or equal to ho.
Ek critical point domain mein woh point hai jahan f dashed zero hai, ya jahan f dashed exist nahi karta.
Jo contrast pakadna hai: local sirf ek chhote neighbourhood ko dekhta hai, jabki absolute poore closed interval a se b par compare karta hai.

sections.title: The First and Second Derivative Tests

board_events.text: The two tests, stated
First Derivative Test — let $c$ be a critical point of a continuous $f$. As $x$ increases through $c$:

board_events.latex: f'\ \text{no sign change}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{point of inflection (no extremum)}

board_events.text: Second Derivative Test \u2014 let $f'(c)=0$ with $f$ twice differentiable at $c$:
Neither test sees endpoints — use the working rule for absolute extrema on $[a,b]$.

segments.text: Here are the two classification tests, stated cleanly for reference.
The First Derivative Test. Let c be a critical point of a continuous function f, and watch the sign of f dashed as x increases through c.
If f dashed goes from positive to negative, c is a local maximum.
If f dashed goes from negative to positive, c is a local minimum.
If f dashed does not change sign at all, c is a point of inflection and there is no extremum there.
The Second Derivative Test. Suppose f dashed at c is zero and f is twice differentiable at c.
Then f double dashed negative gives a maximum, f double dashed positive gives a minimum, and f double dashed zero means the test fails, so you revert to the first test.
One caution stitched to both: neither test sees endpoints, so for absolute extrema on a closed interval you must use the working rule, checking the endpoints as well.
Yeh raha do classification tests, reference ke liye saaf-saaf.
First Derivative Test. Maano c ek continuous function f ka critical point hai, aur f dashed ka sign dekho jaise x, c ke through badhta hai.
Agar f dashed positive se negative jaata hai, c ek local maximum hai.
Agar f dashed negative se positive jaata hai, c ek local minimum hai.
Agar f dashed sign hi nahi badalta, c ek point of inflection hai aur wahan koi extremum nahi.
Second Derivative Test. Maano f dashed at c zero hai aur f, c par twice differentiable hai.
To f double dashed negative maximum deta hai, f double dashed positive minimum deta hai, aur f double dashed zero ka matlab test fail, to aap first test par wapas jaate ho.
Dono se judi ek caution: koi bhi test endpoints nahi dekhta, to closed interval par absolute extrema ke liye working rule use karo, endpoints bhi check karke.

sections.title: Worked example — local values of a cubic

board_events.text: Local max/min of a cubic (CBSE level)
Find local max/min values of $f(x)=2x^3-15x^2+36x+10$.
Local maximum value 38 at $x=2$; local minimum value 37 at $x=3$.
Report the VALUE, not just the location — substitute $c$ back into $f$.

segments.text: Let us run the Second Derivative Test on a clean cubic.
Find the local maximum and minimum values of f of x equals two x cubed minus fifteen x squared plus thirty six x plus ten.
Differentiate: f dashed equals six x squared minus thirty x plus thirty six, which factors as six times x minus two times x minus three, giving critical points x equals two and x equals three.
Compute the second derivative: f double dashed equals twelve x minus thirty.
At x equals two, f double dashed is minus six, which is negative, so this is a local maximum, and the value is f of two, which works out to thirty eight.
At x equals three, f double dashed is six, which is positive, so this is a local minimum, and f of three is thirty seven.
So the local maximum value is thirty eight at x equals two, and the local minimum value is thirty seven at x equals three.
And note the last move: report the value by substituting the critical point back into f, not merely where the extremum sits.
Ek clean cubic par Second Derivative Test chalate hain.
f of x equals two x cubed minus fifteen x squared plus thirty six x plus ten ke local maximum aur minimum values nikaalo.

Differentiate karo: f dashed equals six x squared minus thirty x plus thirty six, jo six times x minus two times x minus three factor hota hai, critical points x equals two aur x equals three dete hue.
Second derivative compute karo: f double dashed equals twelve x minus thirty.
x equals two par, f double dashed minus six hai, jo negative hai, to yeh ek local maximum hai, aur value f of two hai, jo thirty eight banti hai.
x equals three par, f double dashed six hai, jo positive hai, to yeh ek local minimum hai, aur f of three thirty seven hai.
To local maximum value thirty eight hai x equals two par, aur local minimum value thirty seven hai x equals three par.
Aur aakhri move note karo: critical point ko wapas f mein substitute karke value report karo, sirf jagah nahi.

board_events.text: Open box of maximum volume (CBSE HOTS)
A square tin of side 18 cm: cut a square of side $x$ from each corner, fold up. Maximize the volume.

segments.text: This is the famous open-box problem, the classic optimization word problem.
A square sheet of tin of side eighteen centimetres has a small square of side x cut from each corner; the flaps are folded up to form an open box. We want the x that maximizes the volume.
Picture it: after cutting the corners, the base is a square and the folded-up flaps give the height.
After cutting, the base is eighteen minus two x by eighteen minus two x, and the height is x, so the volume is x times eighteen minus two x, all squared, on the feasible domain zero to nine.

Differentiate by the product rule and factor: V dashed equals eighteen minus two x times the bracket eighteen minus two x minus four x, which tidies to eighteen minus two x times eighteen minus six x.
Set V dashed to zero. One root is x equals nine, and the other is x equals three.
Substitute the good root: V of three is three times twelve squared, which is four hundred thirty two centimetres cubed.

The root x equals nine sits on the boundary and gives zero volume, so we reject it. Always test feasibility. The answer: cut three centimetre squares for a maximum volume of four hundred thirty two centimetres cubed.
Yeh famous open-box problem hai, classic optimization word problem.
Ek square tin sheet, side eighteen centimetres, ke har corner se side x ka ek chhota square kaata jaata hai; flaps fold karke ek open box banta hai. Humein woh x chahiye jo volume maximize kare.
Ise socho: corners kaatne ke baad, base ek square hai aur folded-up flaps height dete hain.
Kaatne ke baad, base eighteen minus two x by eighteen minus two x hai, aur height x hai, to volume x times eighteen minus two x, poora squared hai, feasible domain zero se nine par.
Product rule se differentiate karke factor karo: V dashed equals eighteen minus two x times bracket eighteen minus two x minus four x, jo eighteen minus two x times eighteen minus six x banta hai.
V dashed ko zero set karo. Ek root x equals nine hai, aur doosra x equals three.
Achhi root substitute karo: V of three equals three times twelve squared, jo four hundred thirty two centimetres cubed hai.

Root x equals nine boundary par baithti hai aur zero volume deti hai, to use reject karo. Hamesha feasibility test karo. Jawab: three centimetre squares kaato ek maximum volume four hundred thirty two centimetres cubed ke liye.

sections.title: Worked example — absolute extrema on an interval

board_events.text: Absolute extrema on [0, 3] (JEE Main)
Find absolute max/min of $f(x)=3x^4-8x^3+12x^2-48x+25$ on $[0,3]$.
Since $x^2+2>0$ always, the only critical point is $x=2\in(0,3)$.
Absolute max $=25$ at $x=0$ (an endpoint!); absolute min $=-39$ at $x=2$.

segments.text: Now the working rule for absolute extrema, where the endpoints earn their keep.
Find the absolute maximum and minimum of f of x equals three x to the fourth minus eight x cubed plus twelve x squared minus forty eight x plus twenty five, on the interval zero to three.
Differentiate: f dashed equals twelve x cubed minus twenty four x squared plus twenty four x minus forty eight, which factors neatly as twelve times x minus two times the bracket x squared plus two.
Since x squared plus two is always positive, the only critical point is x equals two, and it lies inside the interval.
Now apply the working rule — evaluate at the critical point and both endpoints. First, f of zero is twenty five.
Next, f of two is forty eight minus sixty four plus forty eight minus ninety six plus twenty five, which is minus thirty nine.
And f of three is two hundred forty three minus two hundred sixteen plus one hundred eight minus one hundred forty four plus twenty five, which is sixteen.
Compare the shortlist: the absolute maximum is twenty five, and it sits at the endpoint x equals zero, not at any turning point. The absolute minimum is minus thirty nine at x equals two.
Ab absolute extrema ka working rule, jahan endpoints apni jagah banate hain.
f of x equals three x to the fourth minus eight x cubed plus twelve x squared minus forty eight x plus twenty five ke absolute maximum aur minimum nikaalo, interval zero se three par.
Differentiate karo: f dashed equals twelve x cubed minus twenty four x squared plus twenty four x minus forty eight, jo saaf twelve times x minus two times bracket x squared plus two factor hota hai.
Kyunki x squared plus two hamesha positive hai, ekmaatra critical point x equals two hai, aur yeh interval ke andar hai.
Ab working rule lagao — critical point aur dono endpoints par evaluate karo. Pehle, f of zero twenty five hai.
Aage, f of two equals forty eight minus sixty four plus forty eight minus ninety six plus twenty five, jo minus thirty nine hai.
Aur f of three equals two hundred forty three minus two hundred sixteen plus one hundred eight minus one hundred forty four plus twenty five, jo sixteen hai.
Shortlist compare karo: absolute maximum twenty five hai, aur yeh endpoint x equals zero par baithta hai, kisi turning point par nahi. Absolute minimum minus thirty nine hai x equals two par.

sections.title: Worked example — cylinder inscribed in a sphere

board_events.text: Largest cylinder in a sphere (JEE Advanced)
Greatest-volume cylinder inscribed in a sphere of radius $R$: find its height and that volume.

segments.text: The Advanced-level classic: the largest cylinder you can fit inside a sphere.
Find the height of the cylinder of greatest volume that can be inscribed in a sphere of radius R, and find that maximum volume.
The cylinder's axis passes through the sphere's centre, so a right triangle links the base radius, the half-height, and the sphere radius.
That relation is r squared plus h over two, all squared, equals R squared, which gives r squared equals R squared minus h squared over four.
Write the volume as a single-variable function of h: V equals pi r squared h, which becomes pi times the bracket R squared h minus h cubed over four, on the domain zero to two R.
Differentiate and set to zero: V dashed equals pi times R squared minus three h squared over four, equal to zero, giving h equals two R over root three.
Check the curvature: V double dashed is pi times minus three h over two, which is negative, confirming a maximum.
Substitute back and simplify: the maximum volume is four pi R cubed over three root three, which rationalizes to four root three pi R cubed over nine.
Advanced-level classic: sabse bada cylinder jo aap ek sphere ke andar fit kar sakte ho.
Radius R ke sphere mein inscribe kiye ja sakne waale greatest-volume cylinder ki height nikaalo, aur woh maximum volume bhi.
Cylinder ka axis sphere ke centre se guzarta hai, to ek right triangle base radius, half-height, aur sphere radius ko jodta hai.
Woh relation hai r squared plus h over two, poora squared, equals R squared, jo r squared equals R squared minus h squared over four deta hai.
Volume ko h ka single-variable function likho: V equals pi r squared h, jo pi times bracket R squared h minus h cubed over four ban jaata hai, domain zero se two R par.
Differentiate karke zero set karo: V dashed equals pi times R squared minus three h squared over four, equal to zero, jo h equals two R over root three deta hai.
Curvature check karo: V double dashed pi times minus three h over two hai, jo negative hai, ek maximum confirm karte hue.
Wapas substitute karke simplify karo: maximum volume four pi R cubed over three root three hai, jo rationalize hokar four root three pi R cubed over nine ban jaata hai.

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips — maxima and minima

board_events.text: Pitfalls & pro-tips
Pitfall 1: calling every critical point an extremum \u2014 $f'(c)=0$ is only a candidate (see $x^3$).
Pitfall 2: quitting when the second test fails \u2014 $f''(c)=0$ means 'inconclusive', not 'no extremum'.
Pitfall 3: forgetting endpoints in absolute-extrema problems — the global extreme often lives there.
Pitfall 4: keeping infeasible roots — a negative length or zero volume must be discarded.
Pro-tip: pick your test — clean $f''$ favours the second test; messy $f''$ or corners favour the first.
Always answer the exact question — often the value or a dimension, not the variable you solved for.

segments.text: Let us gather the traps that quietly cost marks in maxima and minima.

Pitfall one: calling every critical point an extremum. f dashed at c equal to zero is only a candidate; always finish with a sign flip or a curvature check. The inflection point of x cubed is the standard trap.

Pitfall two: quitting when the second-derivative test fails. f double dashed at c equal to zero means inconclusive, not no extremum. Go back to the first test — never write no maximum or minimum from a failed second test.
Pitfall three: forgetting the endpoints in absolute-extrema problems. On a closed interval the global extreme often lives at an endpoint, so evaluate f there too.
Pitfall four: keeping infeasible roots. A root giving a negative length or zero volume must be discarded — state the feasible domain first so the rejection is automatic.

Pro-tip: match the test to the function. Polynomials with a clean second derivative favour the Second Derivative Test; messy second derivatives, or non-differentiable corners, favour the First Derivative Test via a sign chart.
<whisper> And the habit that saves marks: always answer the exact question asked, which is often the maximum value or a dimension, not the variable you happened to solve for.

board_events.text: Tangent and normal at a point
The tangent just 'kisses' the curve — its slope matches the curve's slope there.

board_events.text: Since the derivative is the slope, the tangent's slope at $(x_0,y_0)$ is $m=f'(x_0)$.
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent at the same point — the signpost to the tangent's road.
Perpendicular slopes multiply to $-1$, so the normal slope is $-\tfrac{1}{m}$: flip and negate.
If $f'(x_0)=0$ the tangent is horizontal and the normal vertical; always check the point lies on the curve.

segments.text: This appendix is JEE material, off the current board syllabus, but a steady source of Main questions.
The tangent to a curve at a point is the straight line that just kisses the curve there — the line whose slope matches the curve's slope at that exact point.
Every smooth point on a curve has two natural lines through it: one going along the curve, the tangent, and one cutting across it, the normal.
Since the derivative is the slope, the tangent's slope at the point x-naught, y-naught is simply f dashed at x-naught, which we call m.
The normal is the line perpendicular to the tangent at the same point — picture the tangent as the road and the normal as the signpost standing at right angles to it.
Perpendicular slopes multiply to minus one, so once you know the tangent slope m, the normal slope is minus one over m — flip and negate.
Two cautions: if f dashed at the point is zero the tangent is horizontal and the normal vertical, and always confirm the point actually lies on the curve before writing any line.
